comparison: Both evaluate TEM imaging data for encapsulin morphology (C1-C3). OpenEval finds the evidence well-supported with appropriate controls, while Peer Reviewer raises uncertainty about the choice of R. rubrum encapsulins and questions whether there is evidence these are even produced by R. rubrum, challenging the biological relevance of the system.

Both evaluate iron-dependent oligomerization claims (C4-C7). OpenEval finds the evidence supported by multiple complementary techniques (SEC, ICP-MS, SEC-MALLS) but notes limited reproducibility from single protein preparations. Peer Reviewer raises uncertainty about whether the observed effects are truly iron-dependent or confounded by protein concentration effects and assembly critical concentrations.

Both evaluate metal specificity claims (C8-C9). OpenEval finds the analytical SEC and native PAGE data supportive, noting experiments were repeated twice. Peer Reviewer does not challenge these findings, implicitly accepting the metal specificity evidence.

Both evaluate structural determination claims (C10-C13). OpenEval finds the crystallographic data well-supported with good refinement statistics and novel structural findings. Peer Reviewer also accepts the structural data without challenge, though R4 covers additional claims (C14-C19) about metal binding sites.

Both evaluate metal binding site characterization (C14-C18). OpenEval finds the anomalous diffraction data strongly supportive but notes the 'very high affinity' inference from full occupancy is somewhat speculative. Peer Reviewer accepts the structural and metal binding data without challenge. OpenEval R5 also covers C19 which Peer R4 includes.

OpenEval R6 evaluates structural alignment to classical ferritins (C19), finding it well-supported. Peer R4 covers C19 among other structural claims (C10-C19) and accepts all structural data without challenge.

Both evaluate native MS and IM-MS data (C20-C24). OpenEval finds the mass measurements, iron loading, and CCS agreement strongly supportive with good reproducibility. Peer Reviewer does not challenge the MS data or interpretation of iron-dependent assembly, accepting the consistency across solution, gas phase, and crystal structures.

Both evaluate IM-MS data on apo-EncFtn disorder (C25-C26). OpenEval finds the wide charge state distribution and variable CCS values consistent with published criteria for disordered proteins. Peer Reviewer does not challenge this interpretation, accepting the evidence for metal-dependent folding.

OpenEval R9 evaluates CID-MS data showing iron-retaining dimers (C27, C90), finding it supportive of the dimer as the fundamental iron-binding unit. Peer R5 covers C27 among other MS claims and does not challenge the interpretation, accepting the assembly mechanism evidence.

Both evaluate ferroxidase activity assays (C28-C31). OpenEval finds the A315 measurements clearly show enzyme activity with appropriate controls, but notes limited biological reproducibility. Peer Reviewer does not explicitly challenge the activity measurements but raises a methodological concern about whether iron is 'protein coated or simply balls of rust attached to protein fragments.'

Both evaluate ferroxidase complementarity between EncFtn and encapsulin (C32-C33). OpenEval finds the functional complementarity well-demonstrated. Peer Reviewer does not explicitly challenge these findings, though methodological concerns about iron characterization are raised elsewhere.

Both evaluate TEM imaging of mineralization products (C34-C35). OpenEval finds the morphological differences visually clear but notes the 'controlled mineralization' interpretation is somewhat inferential. Peer Reviewer raises significant uncertainty, questioning whether the observed particles represent controlled mineralization or simply 'balls of rust attached to protein fragments,' requesting additional characterization methods.

Both evaluate iron storage capacity claims (C36-C40). OpenEval finds the ferrozine assay data supportive but acknowledges not reaching maximum apoferritin loading. Peer Reviewer strongly challenges these findings, arguing the Fe/protein ratio is actually 66-100 times lower than classical ferritins, contradicting claims of superior storage capacity. Reviewer notes missing control data for 24-subunit ferritin/apoferritin.

Both evaluate mutagenesis data on assembly (C41-C45). OpenEval finds the SEC and native MS data supportive, showing differential behavior of glutamate versus histidine mutants provides mechanistic insight. Peer Reviewer requested mutagenesis experiments and does not challenge the results presented, implicitly accepting them as addressing the request.

Both evaluate crystallographic analysis of mutants (C46-C49). OpenEval finds the structural conservation and loss of metal binding at FOC sites clearly demonstrated. Peer Reviewer does not challenge the structural analysis, accepting the data supporting functional roles of these residues.

Both evaluate ferroxidase activity of mutants (C50-C51). OpenEval finds the differential effects correlate well with structural roles, with complete loss in E62A consistent with its bridging role. Peer Reviewer does not challenge these measurements, which directly address the request for mutagenesis to test ferroxidase activity.

Both evaluate functional complementarity summary claims (C66-C69). OpenEval finds the evidence strongly supports division of labor but notes the apoferritin comparison is limited by suboptimal loading. Peer Reviewer challenges these claims based on the iron loading critique, arguing the Fe/protein ratio is much lower than classical ferritins, contradicting claims of superior function.

Both evaluate structural and functional distinctions from classical ferritins (C72, C75-C76). OpenEval finds the topological inversion clearly demonstrated and the inference that EncFtn cannot store iron well-supported. Peer Reviewer does not challenge this mechanistic interpretation, accepting the structural logic for compartmentalization requirement, though iron loading data issues may affect overall model validity.

Both evaluate structural docking model (C77-C79). OpenEval finds the positioning geometrically consistent and functionally logical but notes this is computational modeling rather than direct experimental evidence. Peer Reviewer does not challenge the structural modeling or proposed arrangement within encapsulin.

Both evaluate metal-dependent assembly mechanism synthesis (C87-C88, C91). OpenEval finds the mechanism well-supported by multiple techniques with cross-phase consistency. Peer Reviewer does not challenge this assembly mechanism, accepting it as supported by MS, SEC, crystallography, and mutagenesis data.

Both evaluate evolutionary hypothesis (C82-C86). OpenEval finds the phylogenetic and structural data interesting but notes the gene duplication hypothesis is speculative, appropriately presented with cautious language. Peer Reviewer raises uncertainty about evolutionary direction, requesting more phylogenetic data and questioning whether EncFer evolved from ferritin rather than vice versa.

Both evaluate mechanistic model for iron trafficking (C73-C74, C92-C93). OpenEval finds the structural observations sound but functional assignments (entry site, exit portal) largely inferential, noting appropriate speculative language. Peer Reviewer raises uncertainty about the mechanism given concerns about iron loading capacity and nature of iron precipitates, questioning whether the model accurately represents system function.

Both evaluate background/context claims about encapsulin systems (C52-C65). OpenEval finds these well-supported by literature citations and sequence analysis. Peer Reviewer does not challenge these established facts but questions similarity to M. xanthus and whether putative iron-binding sites are conserved.

OpenEval R24 evaluates biochemical principles about iron toxicity and compartmentalization (C70-C71), finding them well-established. Peer R14 covers these claims among others (C70-C76) and does not challenge the biochemical rationale for compartmentalization.

OpenEval R25 evaluates stoichiometric calculations (C80-C81), finding them supported but noting actual stoichiometry may differ from theoretical maximum. Peer R15 covers these claims among others (C77-C81) and does not challenge the calculations or comparison to classical ferritin architecture.

OpenEval R26 evaluates limited iron binding capacity of EncFtn alone (C89), finding it well-supported by MS data. Peer R17 covers C89 among other assembly claims and does not challenge this functional distinction from classical ferritins.

OpenEval R27 evaluates the summary conclusion about absolute requirement for encapsulin (C94), finding it justified by dramatic functional differences. Peer R18 covers C94 and notes the 'absolute requirement' is supported by precipitation observations, but raises uncertainty about overall functional significance given iron loading issues.
